content: Haptic technology, derived from the Greek word Haphe meaning touch or contact, involves the use of mechanical stimulation—such as forces, vibrations, or motions—to interface with users through their sense of touch. This technology enables the creation and manipulation of virtual objects, enhances the remote control of machines, and provides new tools for understanding the human sense of touch. In aviation, early haptic devices were used in aircraft with servo systems to simulate missing aerodynamic forces. For example, in older aircraft without servo systems, pilots could feel aerodynamic buffeting in the controls as a warning of an impending stall. Modern systems replicate this feedback using devices like stick shakers, which simulate control vibrations when the aircraft approaches a critical angle of attack. This is an example of haptic feedback. Similarly, force feedback systems have been experimentally applied in excavators, allowing operators to feel obstacles like rocks embedded in soil, improving efficiency and precision. Teleoperators, or remotely controlled robotic tools, utilize haptic feedback to reproduce contact forces for the operator. The first electrically actuated teleoperators were developed in the 1950s by Dr. Raymond C. Goertz at Argonne National Laboratory for handling radioactive materials. Since then, force feedback has been widely adopted in teleoperators for underwater exploration and other applications. In 1988, researchers at Cybernet Systems developed devices that generated forces from computer simulations, enabling realistic training environments. These technologies have since been commercialized, with force feedback integrated into gaming devices like joysticks and steering wheels. In gaming, haptic feedback is now a standard feature in many controllers, such as steering wheels that simulate road resistance or joysticks that vibrate during gameplay. Some concepts, like temperature-changing controllers, have been explored but remain impractical due to cost and power consumption. Instead, manufacturers have implemented features like ventilation systems to enhance user comfort during prolonged use. Haptics has become a critical component of virtual reality systems, adding the sense of touch to visual experiences. Stylus-based haptic rendering is commonly used, allowing users to interact with virtual environments through tools or styluses. Research into haptic simulation has explored methods like vibrating pin arrays to replicate textures and shapes, though these systems are not yet fully realistic. Several haptic APIs, such as Chai3D and OpenHaptics, have been developed to support research and application development. In medicine, haptic interfaces are valuable for training in minimally invasive procedures and remote surgeries. For example, surgeons could perform operations remotely using teleoperators, reducing fatigue and increasing procedural efficiency. Haptic simulators, like the Virtual Haptic Back (VHB), are used in medical education to teach palpatory diagnosis by simulating the physical properties of human anatomy. In ophthalmology, the term haptic refers to the supporting springs that hold artificial lenses in place after cataract surgery. Haptic devices have also appeared in literature, such as Aldous Huxley’s Brave New World, where feelies theaters provided tactile stimulation during entertainment. Similarly, Vernor Vinge’s novel Rainbows End features advanced haptic technologies. In robotics, the Shadow Dextrous Robot Hand (SDRH) replicates the human grip with embedded haptic sensors in its joints and finger pads. Institutions like Carnegie Mellon University and Bielefeld University have used the SDRH to advance understanding of haptic interactions. In the arts, haptics enable real-time interaction with virtual instruments for sound synthesis or graphic design. In design, haptic devices provide touch feedback to designers and modelers, enabling more intuitive and efficient workflows. These tools allow users to feel the surfaces they are sculpting, enhancing the creative process compared to traditional methods.
